title: Killing Me Softly with Your Rubric
author: Terry Underwood, PhD
source: Learning to Read, Reading to Learn
summary: Terry Underwood traces the history of California's CAP rubrics from 1989, arguing that the teacher-built, field-tested rubric of that era was powerful precisely because teachers constructed it themselves, calibrated it collectively at regional scoring sessions, and could trust the data it produced. The CAP rubrics were derived from real student papers in field tests, creating a feedback loop in which 'teaching to the test' actually meant teaching writing in its actual varieties. Underwood argues that today's rubrics, stripped of teacher agency and collective ownership, have lost this power and become bureaucratic compliance tools. The collapse came through NCLB, the Common Core era, and outsourcing of assessment to private companies. The core claim is that the rubric's authority in 1989 flowed upward from the profession -- which is why the data felt trustworthy and meaningful to classroom teachers. Without that agency, the modern rubric misleads administrators into believing assessment is objective while alienating the teachers who could make it useful.
points: The 1989 CAP rubric was derived from analysis of actual student field-test papers by practicing teachers, not constructed in isolation by administrators -- this gave it empirical grounding and professional legitimacy that current rubrics entirely lack.

'Teaching to the test' under CAP was broadening and deepening instruction because the test demanded teaching writing in its actual varieties -- the key insight is that test design determines whether teaching to it narrows or expands the curriculum.

Teacher agency is the 'reservoir of fuel' that made the system work; when assessment authority flowed upward from the profession rather than downward from a state department, teachers were willing to look at and trust external data.

Regional scoring sessions functioned as some of the most powerful professional development many teachers had experienced -- the magic was in collective calibration around actual student writing, not abstract criteria.

Underwood concludes that restoring rubric-based collaborative assessment is now 'unthinkable' at scale -- not wrong, but politically unimaginable -- which he reads as evidence of the boiling-frog effect in education policy.
quotes: A primary criticism of the rubricization of education today is that it misleads administrators and teachers into believing that assessment is entirely objective and measurable.
Developing the rubric meant closely and collectively examining key papers selected from the field test data to articulate legible features evident in papers at each score point.
Teacher agency is the reservoir of fuel that made English departments stop talking about the connections among teaching, writing, and assessment, and start doing.

The assessment's authority flowed upward from the profession rather than downward from a state department. That authority is why the data felt trustworthy. Teachers, normally allergic to external numbers, were willing to look at them.
Ordinarily 'teaching to the test' is an accusation, shorthand for narrowing and drilling. In this case, teaching to the test was widening and deepening instruction.

The instrument rewarded the very thing good writing teachers already wanted to do. The alignment was so clean that improving the metric and improving the child were, for a few years, seen as the same act.

Having participated in several of these sessions as a scorer and as a table leader responsible for calibrating the readers at my table, I recall magic in the air when the chief reader would talk to the collective from notes teachers wrote in the parking lot.
Today's rubrics are criticized for dehumanizing education and prioritizing efficiency over genuine engagement.
